cf.title: Quickselect instead of a heap for ORDER BY ... LIMIT N large bounded sorts

input.subject: Quickselect instead of a heap for ORDER BY ... LIMIT N large bounded sorts

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal or the basic design, and no precedent argues against it. Three fixable level 2 points remain open: the reported LIMIT 1 and 2 slowdown on reversed input (maintenance-fit-1), cost_sort() still charging the heap (maintenance-fit-3), and the EXPLAIN label (standards-compat-1). Someone who knows tuplesort has to decide whether the small-LIMIT slowdown is acceptable. Confidence is medium because v2 and v3 are unreviewed and the numbers come from one machine.

brief.title: Quickselect instead of a heap for bounded sorts (ORDER BY ... LIMIT N)
brief.problem: A bounded sort keeps a heap of N tuples and pays O(log N) comparisons per admitted tuple, so at large LIMIT, or on input that admits most tuples, it can be slower than a full sort. Bounded sorts also turn off abbreviated keys. Users running ORDER BY ... LIMIT with a large N, or on unfavourable input order, are affected.
brief.proposed_design: Tuplesort keeps a buffer of up to Max(2 * N, 1000) tuples and, when it fills, runs quickselect to keep the N smallest and free the rest; incoming tuples are still rejected with one comparison against the largest survivor. At the end the survivors go through tuplesort_sort_memtuples() like an unbounded sort. The heap remains only as a fallback when N tuples alone no longer fit in work_mem.
user_visible_surface: Ties on all sort keys can come out in a different order than before; contrib/cube's test needed a tiebreaker.
debug_topn_quickselect GUC to switch back to the heap (0002, marked not for commit).
debug_topn_context_swap GUC to turn off the experimental context swap (0003, experimental).
New tuplelen callback in the tuplesort variant interface (0003, experimental).
EXPLAIN still reports "top-N heapsort" whichever method ran.
author_claims: About 0.35x to 0.44x of master's time at LIMIT 1M to 2.4M on 5M rows, client-side, including a ~360 ms scan.
On reversed input, gains start small and reach about 0.2x to 0.4x by LIMIT 10000; random input with a small LIMIT matches master.
v2 is still slower at LIMIT 1 and 2 on reversed input (1.13x int8, 1.63x en_US at LIMIT 1).
Peak memory is unchanged; the 1000-tuple floor fits in the initial memtuples array.
Worst case is O(n log n) per prune, via fallback to sorting after 2 * log2(n) rounds.
brief.thread_state: John Naylor replied once: use one method or none, try a buffer floor, and consider Andres' survivor-copy idea; Greg did both in v2 and fixed a contrib/cube tie-order failure in v3. Nobody has reviewed v2 or v3 yet.
unclear: Whether LIMIT 1 and 2 on reversed input will get a running-minimum special case or the regression will be accepted.
Whether cost_sort() will stop charging tuples * log2(2 * N) when quickselect runs.
Whether abbreviated keys will stay on for bounded sorts, given the decision happens in tuplesort_set_bound().
No results yet on aarch64, parallel or incremental sort, very wide tuples, or other machines; the 1000 floor comes from one box.
Whether the tie-order change can break user queries or tests outside contrib/cube that rely on the heap's order.

objections.title: Regression on ORDER BY ... DESC LIMIT 1 over append-ordered tables
objections.failure_scenario: An application runs `select ... order by created_at desc limit 1` on a table with no usable index, and the heap is physically in insert order. Every tuple is admitted, which is the patch's reversed-input case. After upgrade the query is up to 1.6x slower with en_US text keys, and nothing in EXPLAIN shows why.
objections.argument: Message #4 reports v2 at 1.13x for int8 and 1.63x for en_US at LIMIT 1 on reversed input. Reversed input is not an exotic order: it is what a DESC sort over append-only data sees. LIMIT 1 and 2 are among the most common bounded sorts, so the users who pay are not the large-LIMIT users who gain. Message #4 offers a running-minimum special case but does not commit to it.
objections.author_must_show: Will the patch keep master's speed at LIMIT 1 and 2 on reversed input, and with what mechanism?

critic.reasoning: Message #4 reports 1.13x (int8) and 1.63x (en_US) at LIMIT 1 on reversed input, and v3 does not include the running-minimum case. A descending sort over insert-ordered rows admits every tuple, so the scenario is concrete.

objections.title: Cost model still charges the heap the executor no longer runs
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA sees the faster Sort+Limit in benchmarks, but the planner still costs it at tuples * log2(2 * N) and keeps choosing a different plan. If cost_sort() is changed later, plan choices change for every bounded sort, including the LIMIT 1 cases the patch makes slower.
objections.argument: Message #1 asks whether cost_sort() should change and gets no answer; message #2 defers it with EXPLAIN as polish. Executor and cost model would then describe different algorithms, and fixing that later moves plans in a release with no executor change to explain it. EXPLAIN still printing "top-N heapsort" adds to the confusion during support.
objections.author_must_show: What cost_sort() formula matches quickselect, and which plan shapes does it change on the benchmark queries?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 asks whether cost_sort() should change and nobody answers; message #2's "polish" reply was about EXPLAIN only. The gap is a missed plan choice and no regression against master, so it stays fixable.

objections.title: EXPLAIN keeps reporting "top-N heapsort" when quickselect ran
objections.failure_scenario: After upgrade, a DBA reads "Sort Method: top-N heapsort" in EXPLAIN ANALYZE for a LIMIT 1000000 query and tunes work_mem or the query assuming heap behaviour, though quickselect ran. If the label is instead renamed, plan viewers and scripts that match the string misclassify every bounded sort.
objections.argument: v1 to v3 always print the old label, and message #1 asks whether to add a method or reuse the name. Message #2 defers this as polish, but it is a user-visible contract. EXPLAIN text and JSON output feed external tools, and the memory reported for quickselect, with its 1000-tuple floor and heap fallback, means something different from a heap. Either way the change needs a decision that the patch does not yet make.
objections.author_must_show: Will EXPLAIN name the method that actually ran, and if it does, which tools or expected outputs that match "top-N heapsort" would need to change?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 asks this question and message #2 defers it, so no version decides what EXPLAIN reports. The tuning scenario is weak, but a label that names a heap when no heap ran is a real consistency gap.

refuted.title: Patch now carries several strategies after asking for one
refuted.failure_scenario: A later tuplesort change, such as abbreviation for bounded sorts or a bump context, is tested on the quickselect path only. The heap fallback runs in the field only when N tuples outgrow work_mem mid-sort, so a bug there shows up months later as wrong top-N results on some customer's wide rows.
refuted.argument: Message #2 said to use one method or none. v2 keeps the heap as a memory fallback, and message #4 adds a possible running-minimum case for N = 1, which makes three paths that future tuplesort patches must keep correct. One forced regression test covers the fallback, but nothing fails loudly if a later change breaks it under real data. The 1000-tuple floor and the 2 * log2(n) cutoff are tuned on one machine type, and they also become constants to maintain.
refuted.author_must_show: Can the heap fallback be removed, or else shown to be the same path an existing, well-exercised case already takes?

critic.reasoning: The fallback reuses master's heap code, and 0001 has a regression test that forces that path and compares it with a full sort. The running-minimum path is not in any patch version, and the 2 * log2(n) cutoff comes from introselect, not from one machine.

refuted.title: LIMIT 1 and 2 on descending-arriving input get slower
refuted.failure_scenario: A user runs `select ... order by created_at desc limit 1` on an append-only table with no usable index. The seq scan returns rows in ascending insert order, so every tuple is admitted. After upgrade this query runs up to 1.63x slower on en_US text keys, and the user finds out from latency monitoring.
refuted.argument: Message #4 reports v2 at 1.13x (int8) and 1.63x (en_US) at LIMIT 1 on reversed input. The heap is dropped there, so users who never ask for large LIMITs pay for a gain they do not use. "Latest row" queries over insert-ordered heaps are a common shape. The author offers a running-minimum special case, but v3 does not include it and no reviewer has accepted the regression.
refuted.author_must_show: Will the next version include the N = 1 (and N = 2) special case, with numbers showing reversed-input LIMIT 1 and 2 at or below master?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1, which states the same LIMIT 1 and 2 regression on reversed input with the same numbers and scenario.

committability.owner_note: John Naylor replied once in message #2 with design direction; nobody has reviewed v2 or v3. The owner must know tuplesort.c and its memory accounting.
committability.liability: Correct results and no slowdown for every ORDER BY ... LIMIT sort, including the work_mem fallback to the heap, for as long as the code stays in tuplesort.c.
committability.author_follow_up: Good sign: the author posted v2 and v3 within the thread, acted on the review in message #2, and offered to run any requested workload.

priority.reason: The gain is about 0.35x to 0.44x of master's time at large LIMIT and on reversed input from LIMIT 8 up, and the change stays inside tuplesort.c with no new user-facing surface in 0001. The 17 KiB main patch touches a core sort path, so review needs care.

provisional_note: The code was not read, so the quickselect's correctness, its memory accounting against work_mem, and the switch to the heap fallback are unchecked. Behaviour under parallel sort, incremental sort and rescans with a changing bound also could not be judged.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Support empty ranges with bounds information
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch keeps the bounds of empty ranges built from bounds, such as int4range(6,6,'[)'), and returns them from lower() and upper(). A v2 patch restored lower() and upper() and added range_start() and range_end() to expose the stored bounds instead.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the patch breaks the set-theoretic definition of ranges as sets of points, to support a regexp_positions use case. Mark Dilger showed that the changed RANGE_HAS_LBOUND and RANGE_HAS_UBOUND macros make hash_range() give different hashes for empty ranges that compare equal, so even v2 changes semantics. Fixing the hash would leave visibly different values comparing equal, so the author abandoned the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
We had a clean set-theoretic
definition of ranges as sets of points, and with this we would not.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix out-of-bounds with function PQescapeInternal
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the buffer size that PQescapeInternal in libpq allocates on its slow path, adding two bytes per quote or backslash. It followed a Coverity report of an out-of-bounds write in pg_createsubscriber.c.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane replied that each quote or backslash is already counted in input_len, so one extra byte per character is enough. He added an Assert that the buffer is filled exactly, and check-world passed. The author checked with a debugger, found no overrun, called the Coverity warning wrong, and withdrew the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Nonsense.  The quote or backslash is already counted in input_len,
so we need to add just one more.

precedents_retrieved.title: Switch logtape and tuplesort to use int64 instead of long
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes block numbers and related counters in logtape.c, tuplesort, and the BufFile block interface (BufFileSeekBlock, BufFileAppend) from long to int64. On Win64 and 32-bit platforms long is 4 bytes, so temp files there are limited to BLCKSZ * LONG_MAX bytes, about 16TB.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The patch drew only support: Peter Geoghegan favored it, and Tom Lane doubted it was worth the trouble but said he would not stand in the way. The last message registers the patch for the next commitfest, and the thread ends there with the entry withdrawn.

precedents_retrieved.title: Memory-bounded HashAgg
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets HashAgg spill to disk so it stays within work_mem even when the planner underestimates the number of groups. When memory is full, existing groups keep aggregating, tuples for new groups go to partition files, and each file is processed in a later pass. A GUC, enable_hashagg_disk, lets the planner choose HashAgg even when it expects the hash table to exceed memory.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Tomas Vondra argued for hashjoin-like batching and noted that growing transition states such as array_agg are not handled, but in message #38 he called the approach reasonable. The last message says the discussion moved to another thread.

precedents_retrieved.title: Memory accounting towards memory-bounded HashAgg
precedents_retrieved.summary: Jeff Davis proposed tracking allocated memory blocks per memory context, optionally including child contexts, as a base for a memory-bounded HashAgg that can spill to disk. Later versions dropped inheritance and kept only a per-context counter of blocks held, reviewed together with the disk-based HashAgg patch.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier returned it with feedback because the patch was "not there yet" after Tomas Vondra's review. Tomas showed that HashAgg read memory from hashcontext, so by-reference transition states in aggcontext, such as array_agg, were not counted. Measuring aggcontext correctly made a 100-group query about 2 times slower. Earlier reviews reported allocation overhead and an unresolved design question about child contexts.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Hmm. It seems that this patch is not there yet, so marking it as
returned with feedback, especially knowing that the patch is incorrect
by using hascontext as mentioned by Tomas.

precedents_retrieved.title: Memory Accounting (towards memory-bounded HashAgg)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a per-context counter of malloc'd block memory to MemoryContextData, kept current in the memory context code, plus MemoryContextMemAllocated() to read it for one context or sum it over child contexts. It is meant as groundwork for a later HashAgg patch that bounds memory and spills to disk.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers objected to adding overhead to hot paths such as AllocSetAlloc for every user, given a reported 1-3% REINDEX slowdown on a POWER machine. Tom Lane also said HashAgg could track its own memory, and that the mechanism had no use in core yet. Following Robert Haas's view that HashAgg should do its own accounting, as tuplesort.c does, Jeff Davis dropped the patch and moved the work into the HashAgg patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: But I think when it comes to these very hot code paths, extreme conservatism is warranted.

precedents_retrieved.title: Bug: Reading from single byte character column type may cause out of bounds memory reads
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes text_substring() so that it never copies more bytes than the input string holds, even when the last character is wrongly encoded. This stops the out-of-bounds read seen when left() runs on a "char" value that holds the first byte of a multibyte character.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Commit ec62ce55a, from a separate thread, fixed the conversion from "char" to text in HEAD and v15, so that case can no longer be reached. Tom Lane said the patch is therefore unnecessary, and that a fix in text_substring() alone is not enough because many other text functions assume valid encoding. Noah Misch argued that text functions should be safe on invalid text carried forward by pg_upgrade, but Tom Lane said the effort and performance cost were not justified.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think we should reject Aleksander's patch, on the grounds that
it's now unnecessary --- or if you want to argue that it's still
necessary, then it's woefully inadequate, because there are surely
a bunch of other text-processing functions that will also misbehave
on wrongly-encoded data.

precedents_retrieved.title: Avoid obscure DES key buffer loop bounds in pgcrypto
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch replaces the `while (q - (uint8 *) keybuf - 8)` loop conditions in `px_crypt_des()` in pgcrypto's crypt-des.c with for-loops bounded by `sizeof(keybuf)`. The goal is clearer code and a workaround for a spurious gcc-16 -O3 -Wstringop-overflow warning caused by a gcc bug.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. A reviewer marked the patch Ready for Committer in August 2026, and no message raises an objection or explains the withdrawal.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Add single-item cache when looking at topmost XID of a subtrans XID"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Add single-item cache when looking at topmost XID of a subtrans XID"
Reverted commit(s): Add single-item cache when looking at topmost XID of a subtrans XID
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 06f5295 as per issues with this approach, both in
terms of efficiency impact and stability.  First, contrary to the
single-item cache for transaction IDs in transam.c, the cache may finish
by not be hit for a long time, and without an invalidation mechanism to
clear it, it would cause inconsistent results on wraparound for
example.  Second, the use of SubTransGetTopmostTransaction() for the
caching has a limited impact on performance.  SubTransGetParent() could
have more impact, though the benchmarking of the single-item approach
still needs to be proved, particularly under the conditions where SLRU
lookups are stressed in parallel with overflowed snapshots (aka more
than 64 subxids generated, for example).

After discussion with Andres Freund.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
Reverted commit(s): Optimize order of GROUP BY keys
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit db0d67db2401eb6238ccc04c6407a4fd4f985832 and
several follow-on fixes.  The idea of making a cost-based choice
of the order of the sorting columns is not fundamentally unsound,
but it requires cost information and data statistics that we don't
really have.  For example, relying on procost to distinguish the
relative costs of different sort comparators is pretty pointless
so long as most such comparator functions are labeled with cost 1.0.
Moreover, estimating the number of comparisons done by Quicksort
requires more than just an estimate of the number of distinct values
in the input: you also need some idea of the sizes of the larger
groups, if you want an estimate that's good to better than a factor of
three or so.  That's data that's often unknown or not very reliable.
Worse, to arrive at estimates of the number of calls made to the
lower-order-column comparison functions, the code needs to make
estimates of the numbers of distinct values of multiple columns,
which are necessarily even less trustworthy than per-column stats.
Even if all the inputs are perfectly reliable, the cost algorithm
as-implemented cannot offer useful information about how to order
sorting columns beyond the point at which the average group size
is estimated to drop to 1.

Close inspection of the code added by db0d67db2 shows that there
are also multiple small bugs.  These could have been fixed, but
there's not much point if we don't trust the estimates to be
accurate in-principle.

Finally, the changes in cost_sort's behavior made for very large
changes (often a factor of 2 or so) in the cost estimates for all
sorting operations, not only those for multi-column GROUP BY.
That naturally changes plan choices in many situations, and there's
precious little evidence to show that the changes are for the better.
Given the above doubts about whether the new estimates are really
trustworthy, it's hard to summon much confidence that these changes
are better on the average.

Since we're hard up against the release deadline for v15, let's
revert these changes for now.  We can always try again later.

Note: in v15, I left T_PathKeyInfo in place in nodes.h even though
it's unreferenced.  Removing it would be an ABI break, and it seems
a bit late in the release cycle for that.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found: the precedent search returned no row about this idea or a close relative. The thread's earlier discussions do not argue against it. Message #1 cites a 2010 thread on quickselect for median and percentile, which is a different use. Message #1 also cites a July thread where the top-N heap lost to a full sort at a large LIMIT, which supports the problem. Message #1 reports a 2014 point that tuplesort cannot allocate a new structure when it runs out of work_mem; the proposal reuses the existing memtuples array, so that point does not apply. Message #2 points to an earlier idea to copy survivors into a new context, and the experimental 0003 builds on it.

Other points do not hold up from this angle. Tie order on equal keys is unspecified in SQL, and the patch documents it. The debug GUCs are marked not for commit, there is no new syntax, and pg_dump is not involved. The cost_sort() change belongs to the planner angle.

The proposal changes only in-memory tuplesort work for bounded sorts, so it has no persistent or cross-node state. It adds no WAL records, on-disk format change, catalog column or protocol message, and does not affect pg_upgrade or standbys. The tuplelen callback in tuplesort.h is in the experimental 0003, targets a major release, and has no ABI cost outside extensions that define their own tuplesort variants. The tie-order change is a query-result question for other angles.

The proposal changes only how tuplesort picks the N smallest tuples, so it adds no privilege, role, exposure or authentication surface. Worst-case cost from data chosen by an unprivileged user is held to O(n log n) per prune by the fallback to sorting, and peak memory stays within work_mem, so no new denial-of-service path follows from the design.

Fit is good: the change stays inside tuplesort, adds no dependency, and John Naylor, who knows the sort code, has engaged once. The objections concern cost to common small-LIMIT queries and the number of code paths left behind.

No existing feature or extension meets this need. The only user-side workaround is a LIMIT above INT_MAX / 2, which forces a full sort, and message #1 shows quickselect beating it in all but one case. A change to tuplesort's internal top-N algorithm cannot be done from an extension or a hook. The patch replaces the heap and keeps it only as a work_mem fallback, so it adds no second user-facing way to do the same job.

Demand is otherwise shown: ORDER BY ... LIMIT is a core path, message #1 cites an earlier hackers thread where large LIMITs hit this, and reversed input, which is common for insert-ordered tables, gains at LIMIT 8 and above. The objection is limited to who pays at very small N.
